Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Sae2/CtIP prevents R-loop accumulation in eukaryotic cells" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and a Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

Our decision has been reached after consultation between the reviewers. Based on these discussions and the individual reviews below, we regret to inform you that your work will not be considered further for publication in eLife at this moment. We believe that this is very interesting work with exciting results, but it needs further analysis to support the model. However, we would be happy to consider a resubmission of your work, if you can appropriately respond to the reviewers.

As I said, this is an interesting study performed in yeast and human cells to show that CtIP is involved in resolving R-loops in conjunction with XPG. By first observing the ability of Sen1 DNA-RNA helicase, involved in transcription termination, to suppress some of the phenotypes of sae2∆ mutants such as CPT sensitivity and R-loop accumulation in the rDNA, authors conclude that yeast Sae2 is important for R-loop removal. They go on to show that Sae2 is found at sites of high transcription, especially upon treatment with CPT in S phase, and that its deletion leads to transcription-dependent damage sensitivity and Pol II stalling following CPT. Notably, most of these findings also apply for CtIP function in human cells. CtIP depletion triggers sensitivity to CPT that is rescued by Senataxin (the Sen1 human ortholog) overexpression. They find that RNA-DNA hybrids accumulate upon CTIP-loss or XPG-loss at laser-induced damage, based on binding of an mCherry-RNaseH sensor. Moreover, CtIP depletion decreases ssDNA break, suggesting that, as XPG, CtIP contributes to R-loop dissolution by generating a ssDNA break promoting the activity of senataxin and other hybrids helicases. The authors show that CtIP and XPG reduce breaks formed by CPT using both comet assays and LM-PCR. The most puzzling data came from combining both XPG and CtIP depletion, since, although their co-depletion completely abolishes the generation of an ssDNA break, no R-loop accumulate in these conditions. The authors interpret these data, as a lack of R-loop extension in these conditions, that would make them undetectable. Together, these studies lead the authors to propose that XPG and CtIP work in a redundant manner to process R-loops by generating a break at the R-loop site and allowing access of SETX to the hybrids for hybrid resolution. They propose a model by which CtIP would promote cleavage of Flap structures as a step to resolve R-loops.

The work is very interesting and exciting and provides an intriguing model and important function of CTIP to understand. However, additional results are needed to test the model and rule out other possibilities. Several experiments require additional control; all studies with S9.6 should provide the control with RNaseH treatment in vitro to show that the signal is removed (S9.6 also recognizes dsRNA and data must assure that the signal detected corresponds to RNA-DNA hybrid). Although authors use Sen1 to remove R-loops, the data suggest that the terminator function of Sen1 has a role in the suppression of the CPT sensitivity and by extension the R-loops. In addition, the yeast data do not clearly support that RNAPII transcription is the major cause of R-loops. The authors are unable to show hybrids in RNAPII genes, but only in rDNA regions. Of particular note, the authors did not sufficiently establish the proposed order of events which place CtIP and XPG upstream of SETX. Is CtIP or XPG needed for Sen1/SETX to bind the DNA at the sites of hybrid formation, tested using the RNaseH sensor and ChIP assays? This would be one prediction of the model if nuclease processing is needed to generate access for Sen1/SETX. Could indeed the authors rule out that SETX and CtIP are not simply acting to reduce the same hybrid structures (albeit in different ways)? In summary, as it stands the authors need more data to substantiate their conclusions.

Reviewer #1:

This is an interesting study performed in yeast and human cells to show that CtIP is involved in resolving R-loops. By first observing the ability of Sen1 DNA-RNA helicase to suppress some of the phenotypes of sae2∆ mutants such as CPT sensitivity and R-loops detected by a specific antibody, authors conclude that yeast Sae2 is important for R-loop removal. The study is extended to human cells, in which using a parallel approach the authors conclude that CtIP have similar role. In this case, they use laser micro-irradiation and siXPG cells, which allow the authors to propose a model by which CtIP would be able to cleave Flap structures as a step to resolve R-loops. This is a new and a priori unexpected involvement of a DSB processing factor in R-loop removal that merits being considered for publication. However, the study has a number of issues that need to be resolved before it can be published. There are three important points that need to be solved first, apart from the essential experiments suggested below.

- All studies with S9.6, except one in Figure 6A, did not provide the control with RNase H1 to show that the signal is removed. It is known that S9.6 also recognizes dsRNA and it is not possible to make conclusions with this antibody without removing the signal with RNase H1.

- Although authors use Sen1 to remove R-loops, the data suggest that the terminator function of Sen1 has a role in the suppression of the CPT sensitivity and by extension the R-loops. It is necessary to show that RNH1 overexpression, not just Sen1/SETX also suppresses the CPT phenotype in yeast and that of micro-irradiated human cells.

- Authors propose that CtIP/Sae2 may have a new FLAP endonucleolytic function similar to XPG. This conclusion is based on the similar phenotypes observed for CtIP and XPG-depleted cells. However, a similar phenotype may be produced by different mechanisms, and R-loop dynamics may respond to many different factors. The in vivo data showing that in the double depletion in human cells they have equal amount of R-loops than the simple is inconsistent with a model implying that an ssDNA nick (as that caused by S1 in vitro experiment) stabilizes R-loops. The in vivo data do not seem to support the model proposed since if CtIP is not able to cleaves the FLAP structure, R-loops would not be stabilized. In this context, the S1 experiment is really confusing and unnecessary in this study (the Lieber lab already showed in the past that a nick in the DNA increases the accumulation of R-loops).

- Provided the know function of CtIP in DSB resection and the relevance of transcription-replication collisions as a way to produce stalled and collapsed forks and considering the possibility that it could also lead to fork reversal generating a one-ended DSB-like structure susceptible of being resected by CtIP to restart the fork, it may be possible that the inability of CtIP to act at broken or reversal replication forks stalled in front of an R-loop lead to an accumulation of these hybrids as structures causing the lethality in CPT or microirradiation and Sae2/CtIP cells. Consequently, it is necessary to show that in vitro CtIP has the suggested activity. The assay done with S1 should indeed be performed with CtIP.

In Figure 1, authors should show overexpression of RNaseH to demonstrate that R-loops are the cause of CPT sensitivity in sae2∆ strain.

Since the CPT sensitivity phenotype is observed in S-phase, it would be important to address if Sen1 and RNaseH1 rescue sae2∆ sensitivity to HU. Could it be transcription/replication collisions not R-loop dependent?

A DRIP-qPCR analysis of some of the genes with increased Sae2 recruitment in the ChIP-seq to validate the data.

In Figure 1E, the control DRIP samples with RNaseH1 treatment is not shown.

No statistical analysis is supplied for any of the yeast tables. This is essential in Figure 3A, where authors claim that o/e SEN1 reduces RNA Pol II accumulation. Again, an RNaseH1 o/e should be included.

In Figure 4A, authors should show overexpression of RNaseH as a way to demonstrate that R-loops are the cause of CPT sensitivity in cells depleted of CtIP.

Immunofluorescences in Figure 5C should have RNase H -treated cells as control. Image contrast could be improved and also show the channels separately.

How do authors explain the reduction on R-loops compare to siC levels when both nucleases CtIP and XPG are missing? This is odd.

Regarding the ssDNA breaks assay, due to the CtIP role in resection it is expected to have less breaks after DNA damage. Authors could perform the assay in a background known to increase R-loops, such as sen1 or rnh1 rnh2 and see if CtIP depletion reduces the R-loop-dependent DNA breaks.

The yeast data do not seem to support that RNAPII transcription is the major cause of R-loops. The authors are unable to show hybrids in RNAPII genes, but only in rDNA regions. Indeed, it makes sense from the data that CPT, that it is the rDNA region, in which the Tollervey lab has shown the relevance of Top1 to prevent R-loop formation, where the major intermediate leading to lethality may accumulate after CPT. Is there any data showing an involvement of Sen1 in RNAPI transcription termination? This needs to be considered, since at the end it is not really clear which function of Sen1 is able to suppress the sensitivity to CPT of sae2∆ cells.

The enrichment of Sae2 at 176 sites of transcription in S phase may not necessarily related with R-loops. Authors do not show whether such enrichment is reduced by RNase H overexpression. At least should be done by DRIP-qPCR to validate the data using RNase H.

In the genome-wide analysis, the fact that RNAPII is found at high levels at sites previously described to from R-loops does not implies that R-loops are accumulated in sae2∆ strains. It is required to reduce the signal by overexpressing RNH1. Overexpression of Sen1 produces a reduction in signal, but this may be due to the terminator function of Sen1. For this reason, authors need to revert the phenotype with a protein not involved in termination, but just in R-loop removal, such as RNH1.

I am not sure what the results of Figure 4B really says. If CPT causes breaks, it should not be surprising that CtIP increases the sensitivity. Provided the impact of transcription in collisions or increase in damage by other ways, the action of DRB should not be surprising. However, the reduction of the sensitivity phenotype is very small. Results could be repeated using another inhibitor of transcription such as α-amanitin.

In Figure 5 it is necessary to show that all signals are reduced by RNase H.

Reviewer #2:

In this manuscript, Makharashvili et al., report a novel function for Sae2/CtIP in both yeast and human cells: They propose that this endonuclease, known to promote resection during DSB repair, also contributes in R-loops (DNA-RNA hybrids) dissolution, in conjunction with XPG. First, they found that yeast sen1, an RNA-DNA helicase involved in transcription termination, as well as transcription inhibitors, rescue the CPT sensitivity of sae2 deficient strains. They further report that Sae2 binds to highly transcribed genes following exposure to CPT in S phase, that it correlates with accumulation (pausing) of RNA Polymerase II at these positions in CPT treated cells, and that R-loops accumulate in Sae2 deficient strain (at the rDNA locus). Notably, most of these findings also apply for CtIP function in human cells: CtIP depletion triggers sensitivity to CPT that is rescued by Senataxin (the Sen1 human ortholog) overexpression and R-loops accumulate in CtIP-depleted cells, as they do in XPG-depleted cells, as previously reported. Moreover, CtIP depletion decreases ssDNA break, suggesting that, as XPG, CtIP contributes to R-loop dissolution by generating a ssDNA break promoting the activity of senataxin and other hybrids helicases. All these data identify Sae2/CtIP as a key regulator of R-loops stability on yeast and human genome. The most puzzling data came from combining both XPG and CtIP depletion, since, although their co depletion completely abolishes the generation of an ssDNA break, no R-loop accumulate in these conditions. The authors interpret these data, as a lack of R-loop extension in these conditions, that would make them undetectable.

Given the threat of R-loop on genome stability that has been clearly described recently, identifying the mechanisms that function to regulate their occurrence on the genome is of prime interest. Additionally, the model presented here is very interesting and exciting. Yet I feel that (i) the model would be more convincing if the same loci were analyzed across the Figures, (see main point 1 below) and (ii) some key experiment are lacking to fully support the model (see main point 2).

For the yeast part, the authors need to show that indeed, R-loops accumulates at sites that recruit sae2 upon CPT treatment. They show Figure 2E that they do accumulate on rDNA, but to be consistent with Figure 2C, and Figure 3A-B and to demonstrate convincingly the relationship at specific loci between Sae2 and R-loops, the authors need to report the accumulation of R-loops at ENO1, ADH2, FBA1, as well as SNR13, SNR5. Additionally, the authors need to extend their Sae2-flag ChIP-seq data analysis more specifically by comparing their data with DRIP-seq yeast genome profiles (see my detailed points on Figure 2).

For the mammalian cells part, the fact that codepletion of XPG and CtIP shows no R-loops accumulation but deficient ssDNA breakage is really puzzling. The authors propose that the hybrids still accumulate in these conditions but are not detectable using their assay (S9.6 and mutated cherry RNAseH). The author needs to demonstrate that this is the case. Indeed, that CtIP depletion rescues R-loop accumulation in XPG-depleted cells may also indicate that CtIP lies downstream XPG mediated-ssDNA cleavage, hence challenging their model. I realize this may be difficult to assess, but this is an important piece of data that is lacking to support their current model; maybe the authors could try at one locus non denaturing sodium bisulfite treatment to detect ssDNA (as in Ginno et al., 2012 or Loomis et al., 2014)?

Figure 1: Sen 1 also rescues viability upon CPT in mre 11 deficient strain. Can the author comment and integrate the MRX complex in their R-loop processing model?

Figure 2: The ChIP-seq data should be more described, and a full supplemental Figure should be provided. Do the 45 peaks also overlap with the 176 peaks in presence of CPT? If yes, can we see some examples on browser? Can the author show a scatter plot where for each gene, the transcription level is plotted against the CPT-treated enrichment of Sae2 (normalized against gene length)? The author could also retrieve RNA Pol II mapping and perform the same analysis. Another very common way to show this type of data, would be to separate the yeast genes based on their expression level and show that Sae2 binding is statistically higher for the highly expressed genes subset compared to the low expressed set of genes. Finally, Sae2 binding in S phase upon CPT should be compared to DRIP-seq data from the Koshland lab (Wahba et al., 2016). Given that the authors show R-loop accumulation at rDNA, can they also report the change of Sae2 recruitment upon CPT on rDNA from their Sae2 ChIP-seq? Can we also see the snapshot for PDC1, SNR13, SNR5 for Sae2 distribution in CPT treated samples?

Figure 3: "We did not observe CPT induced RNA Pol II pausing at PDC1". It seems from the Figure that the author can actually see some Rbp2 increase (Figure 3B).

Figure 5: In their expression study, is there some overlap between genes modified following CPT treatment and genes modified after CtIP depletion? Can the author directly show the DRIP-seq count on the different gene subsets (WT -vs +CPT, WTvsCtiP -CPT and WT vs CtIP + CPT) compared to random genes (together with p values)?

Figure 6: Part of the Figure 6B, can the author show the R-loop level by DRIP qPCR (only at the b-actin gene) upon XPG and CtIP depletion?

Figure 8: the assay presented Figure 8D is very nice. Could the author also perform XPG only and CtIP/XPG depletion to further validate that indeed ssDNA breakage is absent in these conditions?

Reviewer #3:

In this manuscript, the role of Sae2/CTIP in R-loop accumulation and processing is explored both in yeast and mammalian cells. Motivated by understanding the unexpected sensitivity of Sae2/CTIP-deficient cells to CPT-induced 3'-ssDNA lesions, Paull and colleagues explored the role of transcriptional regulation in survival of Sae2-deficient cells. Upon finding that SEN1 expression rescues this sensitivity and that its loss enhances sensitivity, they go on to show that Sae2 is found at sites of high transcription, especially upon treatment with CPT, and that its deletion leads to transcription-dependent damage sensitivity and Pol II stalling following CPT. Similarly, they find in mammalian cells that sensitivity due to CTIP loss can be rescued by SETX expression and that RNA-DNA hybrids accumulate upon CTIP-loss or XPG-loss at laser-induced damage, based on binding of an mCherry-RNaseH sensor. Hybrids are also elevated in the absence of damage and these nucleases both at genes know to form R-loops and R-loop inducible sites. Finally, the authors show that CtIP and XPG reduce breaks formed by CPT using both comet assays and LM-PCR. Together, these studies lead the authors to propose that XPG and CtIP work in a redundant manner to process R-loops by generating a break at the R-loop site and allowing access of SETX to the hybrids for hybrid resolution.

While this is an intriguing model and important function of CTIP to understand, I think that the model is somewhat premature at this point and additional results are needed to test the model and rule out other possibilities. Several experiments require additional controls as well. Of particular note, I don't think the authors have sufficiently established the proposed order of events which place CtIP and XPG upstream of SETX. Is CtIP or XPG needed for Sen1/SETX to bind the DNA at the sites of hybrid formation, tested using the RNaseH sensor and ChIP assays? This would be one prediction of the model if nuclease processing is needed to generate access for Sen1/SETX. Also, can the authors rule out that SETX and CtIP are not simply acting to reduce the same hybrid structures (albeit in different ways)? As it stands the authors need more data to substantiate their conclusions.

Where does the CPT-induced break fit into the authors' model? The break induced by CtIP/XPG would be in addition to this CPT-induced break. This is omitted from Figures and models and a somewhat confusing point.

Figure 2: As a specificity control the authors should test whether Sae2 binding by ChIP is blocked by transcription inhibition.

Figure 2: Since the DRIP did not work well in yeast, it would be helpful to show that Sae2 binding by ChIP is rescued by overexpression of RNaseH or Sen1 in yeast cells. Similarly, they could ask if RNaseH overexpression rescues CPT effects on survival.

Figure 3: The authors need to analyze several other genes that are not expressed or expressed at lower levels to show specificity of the effect of CtIP loss at highly expressed genes. Right now they examine two genes, PDC1 and NRD1 as negative controls (if I understand this correctly) and Pol II binding is actually elevated at the first site.

Figure 4: Does RNaseH overexpression rescue viability of CTIP deletion? Also, please comment why in Figure 4 hybrids increase with DRB treatment in WT cells?

Figure 4, Figure 5 and Figure 6: Is the nuclease activity of XPG required for any of the observed effects? Testing this in at least one of the assays would be helpful.

Figure 5D: Does RNaseH expression in vivo and RNaseH treatment in vitro reduce the increased hybrid signal (which is actually very weak). This is an important control.

Figure 5E/F: What is the rationale for both increases and decreases in transcription overlapping with site of hybrid formation? I don't understand the implications of the RNA-seq data. Also, Figure 5F is missing in the Figure, making these data difficult to evaluate.

Figure 5: What is the impact of CtIP and XPG loss, or loss of both, on the cell cycle. Are breaks or hybrid levels reduced due to alterations in cell cycle progression (e.g. failure to enter S phase) or accumulation in G2. It seems in WT cells hybrids are naturally higher in G2 and if breaks depend on S phase entry changes in cell cycle could affect the interpretation.

Figure 6: Why are there no more breaks upon addition of CPT? Shouldn't the CPT itself lead to break formation even without the action of XPG and CtIP? Also, alkaline comet is not specific for SSB detection – these could be DSBs. I suggest the authors use caution in the way they present these data.

The idea that the R-loops are too small to be detected when both XPG and CtIP are lost is not well supported. Isn't it possible that there is no R-loop under these conditions and that RNAPII has simply stalled and is the toxic lesion? Can RNaseH expression rescue sensitivity due to loss of both XPG and CtIP? That is one test of this idea. Or can evidence for a smaller R-loops be obtained using bisulfite sequencing. Minimally I think other models should be considered.

Thank you for submitting your article "Sae2/CtIP prevents R-loop accumulation in eukaryotic cells" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by the same three peer reviewers that revised the first submission, and the evaluation has been overseen by the same Reviewing Editor and Jessica Tyler as the Senior Editor. Summary:

Makharashvili et al., report a novel function for Sae2/CtIP in both yeast and human cells, and propose that Sae2/CtIP, known to promote resection during DSB repair, also contributes in R-loop (DNA-RNA hybrids) dissolution, in conjunction with XPG. In this revised version, the authors have addressed to a reasonable extent my main points. More specifically they are now consistent throughout the manuscript, and report Sae2 binding and R-loop accumulation in Sae2 deleted strain at the same loci. They have also now changed their discussion to take more hypotheses into account. They have also largely controlled their data by performing RNAseH treatment to validate their results obtained with S9.6 antibody. This manuscript is a significantly improved version of the previous one. Results are now clearer and convincing. However, the key conclusion of their model that CtIP cleaves the loop needs further support and clarification before acceptance.

Essential revisions:

The results on which the model proposed rely on CPT-treated cells (i.e. Figure 2A-E, Figure 4A-C, Figure 5F and Figure 8) (CPT creates ssDNA breaks with Top1-cc) or cells upon laser-induced breaks (i.e. Figure 4D-H). So, the experimental conditions used implies to start with a genotoxic-induced break. It is still therefore unclear why CtIP would be required for an additional break. Indeed, authors were not able to show the proposed activity of CtIP in vitro. Authors would need to show the action of CtIP in untreated cells (no CPT, no laser irradiation), with no break, to support their model that demands that CtIP cleaves the loop. The known action of the Sae2/CtIP nuclease activity on DNA resection as a requirement to remove the RNA-DNA hybrid accumulated at a break would make much more sense and fit better with the combined effect with XPG. Therefore, either authors provide new data with untreated cells to support their model as such or alternatively include in their model the breaks caused by CPT/laser irradiation to explain the role of CtIP under such conditions.

claims.claim: Obvious pausing of RNA Pol II in the absence of Sae2 was induced by CPT at the snoRNA genes SNR13 and SNR5 and the associated gene TRS31.
claims.source: Obvious pausing of RNA Pol II in the absence of Sae2 was also induced by CPT at the snoRNA genes SNR13 and SNR5 and the associated gene TRS31 (Figure 3B), which have been shown to be transcribed by RNA Pol II and exhibit termination read-through, altered RNA Pol II occupancy, and R-loops in the absence of Sen1 function (Steinmetz et al., 2006; Grzechnik et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Sen1 is present at ADH1, ENO2, and FBA1 sites in the absence of SAE2.
claims.source: This showed that Sen1 is present at these sites (ADH1, ENO2, FBA1) in the absence of SAE2 (Figure 3C), thus the binding of the helicase to these sites is Sae2-independent.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The binding of Sen1 to ADH1, ENO2, and FBA1 sites is Sae2-independent.
claims.source: This showed that Sen1 is present at these sites (ADH1, ENO2, FBA1) in the absence of SAE2 (Figure 3C), thus the binding of the helicase to these sites is Sae2-independent.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Sen1 is present at these sites in the absence of SAE2.

claims.claim: Depletion of CtIP greatly diminishes cell survival in the presence of CPT.
claims.source: As expected, depletion of CtIP greatly diminishes cell survival in the presence of CPT, and re-expression of wild-type CtIP rescues the CPT sensitivity (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Re-expression of wild-type CtIP rescues the CPT sensitivity in CtIP-depleted cells.
claims.source: As expected, depletion of CtIP greatly diminishes cell survival in the presence of CPT, and re-expression of wild-type CtIP rescues the CPT sensitivity (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Overexpression of Senataxin in the CtIP-depleted cells completely rescues the CPT sensitivity.
claims.source: Remarkably, overexpression of Senataxin in the CtIP-depleted cells completely rescues the CPT sensitivity; however, unlike the yeast experiments, no effect of human PCF11 expression was detected (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: No effect of human PCF11 expression was detected on CPT sensitivity in CtIP-depleted cells.
claims.source: Remarkably, overexpression of Senataxin in the CtIP-depleted cells completely rescues the CPT sensitivity; however, unlike the yeast experiments, no effect of human PCF11 expression was detected (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Pre-treatment of cells with DRB partially rescues the CPT sensitivity caused by CtIP deficiency.
claims.source: Indeed, we observe that pre-treatment of the cells with DRB, an inhibitor of RNA polymerase II-dependent RNA synthesis, partially rescues the CPT sensitivity caused by CtIP deficiency (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The recruitment of RNaseH occurs to a higher intensity in CtIP-depleted cells in comparison to cells complemented with wild-type CtIP.
claims.source: Measurement of the accumulation of RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry signal over time in these cells showed that the recruitment of RNaseH occurs to a higher intensity in CtIP-depleted cells in comparison to cells complemented with wild-type CtIP, suggesting that higher levels of R-loops are formed in the absence of CtIP (Figure 4C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claims.claim: Higher levels of R-loops are formed in the absence of CtIP.
claims.source: Measurement of the accumulation of RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry signal over time in these cells showed that the recruitment of RNaseH occurs to a higher intensity in CtIP-depleted cells in comparison to cells complemented with wild-type CtIP, suggesting that higher levels of R-loops are formed in the absence of CtIP (Figure 4C,D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of higher RNaseH recruitment in CtIP-depleted cells.

claims.claim: With Senataxin expression, the recruitment of RNaseH in the CtIP-depleted cells is reduced to the levels observed in cells expressing wild-type CtIP.
claims.source: We expressed the C-terminal domains of human Senataxin in the CtIP-depleted cells, and measured the levels of laser-induced R-loops by the live cell imaging method. Here also we found that with Senataxin expression, the recruitment of RNaseH in the CtIP-depleted cells is reduced to the levels observed in cells expressing wild-type CtIP (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The NA/HA mutant of CtIP failed to reduce the increased RNaseH recruitment to damage sites that occurs in CtIP-deficient cells.
claims.source: Here we used the N289A/H290A (NA/HA) mutant allele also containing shRNA-resistant mutations to complement CtIP-depleted cells and found that this mutant failed to reduce the increased RNaseH recruitment to damage sites that occurs in CtIP-deficient cells (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The nuclease activity of CtIP appears to play a role in DNA damage recognition and/or processing that helps to prevent R-loop accumulation in human cells.
claims.source: Thus the nuclease activity of CtIP appears to play a role in DNA damage recognition and/or processing that helps to prevent R-loop accumulation in human cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the nuclease-deficient mutant fails to reduce R-loop accumulation.

claims.claim: Inhibition of transcription rescues the R-loop accumulation phenotype caused by CtIP deficiency.
claims.source: To further test the role of active transcription in R-loop accumulation, we pre-treated cells with 5,6-dichloro-1-beta-D-ribofuranosylbenzimidazole (DRB), a RNA polymerase II inhibitor, and found that inhibition of transcription rescues the R-loop accumulation phenotype caused by CtIP deficiency (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: U2OS cells depleted of Senataxin exhibit increased R-loop formation after laser-induced DNA damage.
claims.source: Indeed, U2OS cells depleted of Senataxin also exhibit increased R-loop formation after laser-induced DNA damage (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous observations of DNA damage sensitivity in Senataxin mutant cells (Suraweera et al., 2007; Lavin et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: XPG deficient cells accumulate more R-loops after laser induced DNA breaks in comparison to wild-type cells.
claims.source: As expected, we observed that the XPG deficient cells accumulate more R-loops after laser induced DNA breaks in comparison to wild-type cells (Figure 4G, S2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Concurrent depletion of both CtIP and XPG showed R-loops at levels comparable to wild-type untreated cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, however, concurrent depletion of both CtIP and XPG showed R-loops at levels comparable to wild-type untreated cells (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: R-loops do not form efficiently in the absence of both CtIP and XPG, or they are not recognized efficiently by the RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry protein in the absence of both CtIP and XPG.
claims.source: This result suggests that R-loops do not form efficiently in the absence of both CtIP and XPG, or that they are not recognized efficiently by the RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry protein in the absence of both CtIP and XPG.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the observation that R-loops are at wild-type levels in double-depleted cells.

claims.claim: CtIP-depleted U2OS cells show a statistically significant increase in RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry fluorescence intensity in all cell cycle phases.
claims.source: Using this procedure, unbound RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry protein is removed from the nucleoplasm by detergent extraction, while protein bound to chromatin is retained. This analysis showed a statistically significant increase in RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry fluorescence intensity in CtIP-depleted U2OS cells in all cell cycle phases (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The levels of RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry fluorescence intensity in CtIP-depleted cells complemented with the nuclease-deficient form of CtIP (NA/HA) are identical to that of CtIP-depleted cells.
claims.source: Similarly, we examined R-loop accumulation in CtIP-depleted cells complemented with the nuclease-deficient form of CtIP (N289A/H290A, NA/HA, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and found the levels of RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry fluorescence intensity identical to that of CtIP-depleted cells (Figure 5B), suggesting that the nuclease activity of CtIP is necessary for R-loop resolution even in cells that are not exposed to exogenous damage.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The nuclease activity of CtIP is necessary for R-loop resolution even in cells that are not exposed to exogenous damage.
claims.source: Similarly, we examined R-loop accumulation in CtIP-depleted cells complemented with the nuclease-deficient form of CtIP (N289A/H290A, NA/HA, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and found the levels of RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry fluorescence intensity identical to that of CtIP-depleted cells (Figure 5B), suggesting that the nuclease activity of CtIP is necessary for R-loop resolution even in cells that are not exposed to exogenous damage.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the nuclease-deficient mutant shows the same R-loop levels as CtIP-depleted cells.

claims.claim: Undamaged CtIP-depleted or XPG-depleted cells have significantly more R-loops than their wild-type counterparts.
claims.source: We found that undamaged CtIP-depleted or XPG-depleted cells have significantly more R-loops than their wild-type counterparts (Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: Concurrent depletion of CtIP and XPG resulted in a lower level of R-loop accumulation.
claims.source: We also observed that concurrent depletion of CtIP and XPG resulted in a lower level of R-loop accumulation (Figure 5D), similar to the result with laser-induced damage (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: CtIP depletion was found to alter 5013 (~16%) of transcripts, with both increases (2,578) and decreases (2,435) observed relative to the control cells.
claims.source: CtIP depletion was found to alter 5013 (~16%) of these transcripts, with both increases (2,578) and decreases (2,435) observed relative to the control cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq analysis.

claims.claim: 1285 transcripts were upregulated upon CPT treatment, and 1158 transcripts were downregulated.
claims.source: We found that there are transcriptional changes associated with CPT exposure in U2OS cells: 1285 transcripts were upregulated upon CPT treatment, and 1158 transcripts were downregulated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq analysis.

claims.claim: Over 60% of the genes affected by CPT overlap with R-loop prone regions of the genome.
claims.source: Over 60% of the genes affected by CPT (either up or down) overlap with R-loop prone regions of the genome (Ginno et al., 2012) (see 'WT only, - vs +CPT', Figure 5F), whereas less than 40% overlap with DNA-RNA immunoprecipitation (DRIP) positive genes occurs with a randomized control.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Depletion of CtIP has effects on transcription that are correlated with R-loop-prone regions of the genome.
claims.source: A similar analysis of the gene set identified in CtIP-depleted cells compared to normal cells also indicates a higher than expected overlap (~50%), suggesting that depletion of CtIP has effects on transcription that are correlated with R-loop-prone regions of the genome.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of higher than expected overlap with R-loop-prone regions.

claims.claim: The levels of R-loops increase with doxycycline-induced transcription at the mouse class switch region (Sγ3).
claims.source: We performed DRIP with the S9.6 antibody followed by quantitative PCR for this locus in U2OS cells and found that the levels of R-loops increase with doxycycline-induced transcription, even in wild-type cells (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: A much larger increase in R-loops was found in CtIP-depleted cells at the Sγ3 locus.
claims.source: A much larger increase in R-loops was found in CtIP-depleted cells, however, while the overall levels of transcripts are similar in both cases (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Higher levels of RNA-DNA hybrids were observed at the β-actin gene in CtIP-depleted cells in the absence of exogenous DNA damage.
claims.source: We observed higher levels of RNA-DNA hybrids at these regions in CtIP-depleted cells in the absence of exogenous DNA damage, which could be reduced to wild-type levels by overexpression of wild-type RNaseH (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: RNA-DNA hybrids at the β-actin gene in CtIP-depleted cells could be reduced to wild-type levels by overexpression of wild-type RNaseH.
claims.source: We observed higher levels of RNA-DNA hybrids at these regions in CtIP-depleted cells in the absence of exogenous DNA damage, which could be reduced to wild-type levels by overexpression of wild-type RNaseH (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: XPG-depleted cells showed an even higher level of R-loops at the β-actin gene.
claims.source: We also tested XPG-depleted cells and observed an even higher level of R-loops under these conditions (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Significantly higher levels of R-loops were found in CtIP-depleted cells at the RPL13A gene.
claims.source: We tested three locations throughout the body of the RPL13A gene and found significantly higher levels of R-loops in CtIP-depleted cells which were reduced by overexpression of RNaseH in cells (Figure 6D) or by treatment of genomic DNA with RNaseH in vitro prior to the immunoprecipitation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: R-loops at the RPL13A gene in CtIP-depleted cells were reduced by overexpression of RNaseH in cells.
claims.source: We tested three locations throughout the body of the RPL13A gene and found significantly higher levels of R-loops in CtIP-depleted cells which were reduced by overexpression of RNaseH in cells (Figure 6D) or by treatment of genomic DNA with RNaseH in vitro prior to the immunoprecipitation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: High levels of R-loops were observed at the RPL13A gene in XPG-depleted cells compared to wild-type.
claims.source: We also observed high levels of R-loops at this gene in XPG-depleted cells compared to wild-type (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: R-loops were approximately 1.5 to 2-fold higher in cells expressing the nuclease-deficient NA/HA allele of CtIP in comparison to cells expressing the wild-type allele.
claims.source: Lastly, the nuclease-deficient NA/HA allele of CtIP was expressed in CtIP-depleted cells, and R-loops were found to be approximately 1.5 to 2-fold higher in these cells in comparison to cells expressing the wild-type allele, similar to our observations in uncomplemented cells (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Depletion of CtIP or XPG increases Senataxin occupancy at the inducible (Sγ3) locus by 3 to 5-fold.
claims.source: Here we asked whether Senataxin is recruited to R-loops in the absence of CtIP or XPG and found that depletion of either factor increases Senataxin occupancy at the inducible (Sγ3) locus (Figure 6G) by 3 to 5-fold, similar to our observations of Sen1 in yeast.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: CtIP depletion led to a significant reduction in the accumulation of DNA breaks after CPT treatment.
claims.source: We found that exposure to CPT generated a marked increase in DNA breaks, and that transcription promotes these breaks, as pretreatment with DRB reduced the levels of breaks by ~75% in wild-type cells (Figure 8A). CtIP depletion led to a significant reduction in the accumulation of DNA breaks after CPT treatment, consistent with the proposed model that CtIP can facilitate the conversion of stalled transcription associated DNA lesions into DNA breaks.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Transcription promotes DNA breaks after CPT exposure.
claims.source: We found that exposure to CPT generated a marked increase in DNA breaks, and that transcription promotes these breaks, as pretreatment with DRB reduced the levels of breaks by ~75% in wild-type cells (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: In cells depleted for XPG there are fewer breaks after CPT treatment.
claims.source: In cells depleted for XPG there are fewer breaks after CPT treatment, and in cells depleted for both proteins, we observed no increase in breaks at all with CPT exposure (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: In cells depleted for both CtIP and XPG, no increase in breaks was observed with CPT exposure.
claims.source: In cells depleted for XPG there are fewer breaks after CPT treatment, and in cells depleted for both proteins, we observed no increase in breaks at all with CPT exposure (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Cells expressing the nuclease-deficient NA/HA CtIP mutant showed a large reduction in breaks formed with CPT exposure.
claims.source: To test this, we also examined breaks by comet assay in cells expressing the nuclease-deficient NA/HA CtIP mutant and found that in this case also, there was a large reduction in breaks formed with CPT exposure, very similar to the uncomplemented cells (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The level of single-strand breaks on the template strand of the RPL13A gene was reduced by 40% to 50% with depletion of CtIP.
claims.source: Using this procedure, we did observe spontaneous single-strand breaks on the template strand of the RPL13A gene, and the level of breaks was reduced by 40% to 50% with depletion of CtIP, again consistent with the observation that single-strand breaks are reduced in cells lacking CtIP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: Sae2/CtIP is not only a double-strand break resection factor, but also functions at transcription-associated lesions in eukaryotic cells.
claims.source: These results suggest that Sae2/CtIP is not only a double-strand break resection factor, but also functions at transcription-associated lesions in eukaryotic cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Sen1 acts to remove R-loops from genomic loci.
claims.source: Since the Sen1 helicase acts to remove R-loops from genomic loci, we also tested whether sae2Δ strains show synthetic sensitivity to CPT in combination with deletions of RNase H enzymes which remove ribonucleotides from DNA.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Sen1 function.

claims.claim: Sen1 plays a role downstream of Sae2.
claims.source: Alternatively, it is possible that Sen1 plays a role downstream of Sae2 and that in the absence of Sae2 function, Sen1 catalytic activity is less efficient even though its recruitment to damage sites appears to be unimpeded.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between Sen1 and Sae2.

claims.claim: Loss of CtIP is lethal in mammalian cells.
claims.source: In mammalian cells, loss of CtIP is lethal whereas yeast strains lacking SAE2 have no growth deficit in the absence of DNA damage (McKee and Kleckner, 1997; Prinz et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2005; Makharashvili and Paull, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Yeast strains lacking SAE2 have no growth deficit in the absence of DNA damage.
claims.source: In mammalian cells, loss of CtIP is lethal whereas yeast strains lacking SAE2 have no growth deficit in the absence of DNA damage (McKee and Kleckner, 1997; Prinz et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2005; Makharashvili and Paull, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: CtIP and Sae2 exhibit an intrinsic endonuclease activity that is specific for 5' flap structures.
claims.source: CtIP and Sae2 exhibit an intrinsic endonuclease activity that is specific for 5ʹ flap structures and can be genetically separated from its ability to stimulate the nuclease of activity of Mre11 (Makharashvili et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Arora et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The endonuclease activity of CtIP/Sae2 can be genetically separated from its ability to stimulate the nuclease activity of Mre11.
claims.source: CtIP and Sae2 exhibit an intrinsic endonuclease activity that is specific for 5ʹ flap structures and can be genetically separated from its ability to stimulate the nuclease of activity of Mre11 (Makharashvili et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Arora et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: XPG is an endonuclease that acts in nucleotide excision repair.
claims.source: Since we also show in this work that R-loop formation in CtIP-depleted cells resembles that of cells depleted of XPG, an endonuclease that also acts in nucleotide excision repair, it is possible that both enzymes target 5ʹ flap structures, of which there are at least two present in every R-loop structure (see model in Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about XPG function.

claims.claim: Both CtIP and XPG may target 5' flap structures present in R-loop structures.
claims.source: Since we also show in this work that R-loop formation in CtIP-depleted cells resembles that of cells depleted of XPG, an endonuclease that also acts in nucleotide excision repair, it is possible that both enzymes target 5ʹ flap structures, of which there are at least two present in every R-loop structure (see model in Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that both enzymes have similar effects on R-loop accumulation.

claims.claim: There are at least two 5' flap structures present in every R-loop structure.
claims.source: Since we also show in this work that R-loop formation in CtIP-depleted cells resembles that of cells depleted of XPG, an endonuclease that also acts in nucleotide excision repair, it is possible that both enzymes target 5ʹ flap structures, of which there are at least two present in every R-loop structure (see model in Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of R-loops.

claims.claim: In the absence of both CtIP and XPG, unprocessed nascent R-loops and/or stalled RNA polymerase complexes accumulate.
claims.source: To explain this finding we propose that, in the absence of both CtIP and XPG, unprocessed nascent R-loops and/or stalled RNA polymerase complexes accumulate (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model to explain the observation of lower R-loops in double-depleted cells.

claims.claim: Nascent R-loop structures are small and are not efficiently recognized by either the S9.6 antibody or by RNase H due to topological constraints.
claims.source: We propose that, due to the topological constraints on R-loop formation, these nascent R-loop structures are small and are not efficiently recognized by either the S9.6 antibody or by RNase H.
claims.evidence: This is speculation to explain the observation of lower R-loops in double-depleted cells.

claims.claim: A nick in the non-template strand greatly improves the efficiency of stable R-loop formation.
claims.source: The idea that a nascent R-loop is topologically constrained and relatively inaccessible in the absence of strand breaks is consistent with previous work showing that a nick in the non-template strand greatly improves the efficiency of stable R-loop formation, because the non-template strand then does not compete with the RNA for hybridization to the template strand (Roy et al., 2010; Aguilera and Gómez-González, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Cleavage of one of the DNA strands facilitates removal of the RNA-DNA hybrid by transcription-associated helicases such as Senataxin and/or Aquarius.
claims.source: We propose that cleavage of one of the DNA strands, although seemingly detrimental in its stabilization of the RNA-DNA hybrid, likely facilitates removal of the hybrid by transcription-associated helicases such as Senataxin and/or Aquarius.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: The helicase domain of yeast Sen1 requires single-stranded DNA adjacent to the hybrid for efficient loading prior to unwinding of the annealed RNA.
claims.source: Biochemical characterization of the helicase domain of yeast Sen1 showed that the enzyme requires single-stranded DNA adjacent to the hybrid for efficient loading prior to unwinding of the annealed RNA (Martin-Tumasz and Brow, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Treatment of chromatin with low levels of the single-strand DNA-specific S1 nuclease greatly improves the yield of R-loops immunoprecipitated by the S9.6 antibody.
claims.source: In addition, a recent study found that treatment of chromatin with low levels of the single-strand DNA-specific S1 nuclease greatly improves the yield of R-loops immunoprecipitated by the S9.6 antibody (Wahba et al., 2016), consistent with this hypothesis.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: R-loops greatly increase the level of genomic instability at locations where they accumulate.
claims.source: One possibility is that double-strand breaks form at sites of transcription-replication collisions, since we know that R-loops greatly increase the level of genomic instability at locations where they accumulate, and double-strand breaks have been implicated in these events (Richard and Manley, 2017; Wickramasinghe and Venkitaraman, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: R-loops form in human cells at DNA sites adjacent to induced double-strand breaks.
claims.source: Recent work demonstrates that R-loops form in human cells at DNA sites adjacent to induced double-strand breaks and that the Senataxin enzyme promotes their removal as well as Rad51 recruitment and homologous recombination (Cohen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: A subset of R-loops in yeast induce Rad52-bound double-strand breaks.
claims.source: In addition, a subset of R-loops in yeast were shown to induce Rad52-bound double-strand breaks, with the RNA-DNA hybrid located on one side of the break and resected DNA on the other (Costantino and Koshland, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Double-strand breaks have been shown to accompany high levels of transcriptional activity and appear to facilitate gene expression.
claims.source: Lastly, double-strand breaks have been shown in some contexts to accompany high levels of transcriptional activity and appear to facilitate gene expression (Madabhushi et al., 2015); in this case TopII was implicated in formation of the breaks, but it is not clear if processing of the breaks occurs at these sites or is important for cell survival.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: CtIP was originally identified as a binding partner of C-terminal Binding Protein (CtBP), a transcriptional co-regulator.
claims.source: CtIP was originally identified as a binding partner of C-terminal Binding Protein (CtBP), a transcriptional co-regulator (Schaeper et al., 1998), and also binds directly to Rb and the tumor suppressor BRCA1 which also has been widely reported to affect transcription and R-loop formation (Monteiro et al., 1996; Scully et al., 1997; Takaoka and Miki, 2018; Yu et al., 1998; Hatchi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: CtIP binds directly to Rb and the tumor suppressor BRCA1.
claims.source: CtIP was originally identified as a binding partner of C-terminal Binding Protein (CtBP), a transcriptional co-regulator (Schaeper et al., 1998), and also binds directly to Rb and the tumor suppressor BRCA1 which also has been widely reported to affect transcription and R-loop formation (Monteiro et al., 1996; Scully et al., 1997; Takaoka and Miki, 2018; Yu et al., 1998; Hatchi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: BRCA1 has been widely reported to affect transcription and R-loop formation.
claims.source: CtIP was originally identified as a binding partner of C-terminal Binding Protein (CtBP), a transcriptional co-regulator (Schaeper et al., 1998), and also binds directly to Rb and the tumor suppressor BRCA1 which also has been widely reported to affect transcription and R-loop formation (Monteiro et al., 1996; Scully et al., 1997; Takaoka and Miki, 2018; Yu et al., 1998; Hatchi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: BRCA1 localizes to a subset of transcription termination regions and regulates levels of RNA-DNA hybrids in human cells.
claims.source: BRCA1 itself has been shown to localize to a subset of transcription termination regions and to regulate levels of RNA-DNA hybrids in human cells (Hatchi et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: XPG was recently found to be present in a complex with BRCA1 that is important for cellular responses to DNA damage.
claims.source: In addition, XPG was recently found to be present in a complex with BRCA1 that is important for cellular responses to DNA damage that is separate from its roles in excision repair (Trego et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: CtIP has been shown to have important repair functions in G1 phase cells.
claims.source: Lastly, CtIP has been shown to have important repair functions in G1 phase cells (Barton et al., 2014; Biehs et al., 2017; Helmink et al., 2011; Quennet et al., 2011; Yun and Hiom, 2009); it will be important to determine if the R-loop processing functions indicated here play a role in the repair of transcription-associated damage even outside of S phase and whether this accounts for any of the essential functions of CtIP in mammals.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

results.result: Overexpression of Sen1 or PCF11 rescues DNA damage sensitivity in sae2Δ yeast strains. Sen1 overexpression markedly improved survival of sae2Δ strains to CPT and MMS, with the effect also observed in mre11-H125N mutants. The helicase domain mutation G1747D reduced rescue ability, while R302W had no effect. PCF11 improved CPT survival but other transcription factors (SSU72, RTT103, NRD1, YSH1) showed little effect. Sen1 overexpression did not affect DNA end resection efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C48 provide consistent experimental evidence from multiple genetic backgrounds (sae2Δ, mre11-H125N, double mutants) showing Sen1 and PCF11 rescue effects. The separation-of-function analysis with Sen1 mutants (C43-C47) supports the mechanistic interpretation that helicase/termination activity is important. The resection assay control (C48) appropriately demonstrates specificity of the rescue effect.

results.result: Genetic interactions demonstrate synthetic sensitivity between sae2Δ and factors involved in RNA-DNA hybrid metabolism. The sen1-1 sae2Δ double mutant shows extreme sensitivity to CPT and MMS. Deletion of RNase H enzymes (Δrnh1 Δrnh201) exacerbates DNA damage sensitivity in sae2Δ strains, while RNH1 overexpression partially rescues sae2Δ survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C52, and C53 demonstrate consistent genetic interactions between SAE2 and RNA-DNA hybrid processing factors. The bidirectional genetic evidence (synthetic lethality with deletions, rescue with overexpression) provides strong support for a functional relationship between Sae2 and R-loop metabolism.

results.result: CPT sensitivity in sae2Δ strains is S-phase specific and transcription-dependent. The sae2Δ strain showed marked CPT sensitivity specifically during S phase exposure, and transcription inhibition with thiolutin completely rescued this sensitivity to wild-type levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 provide clear cell cycle-specific and transcription-dependence data. The S-phase specificity (C54) and complete rescue by transcription inhibition (C56) strongly support the interpretation that transcription-replication conflicts underlie the sae2Δ phenotype. The experimental design with synchronized cells is appropriate.

results.result: Sae2 occupancy is enriched at highly transcribed genes during S phase with CPT treatment. ChIP-seq identified 176 Sae2 peaks in S phase with CPT (versus 45 without CPT), enriched at the top 10% of highly transcribed genes but not at replication origins. Enrichment was S-phase and CPT-specific, with ~20% of peaks overlapping known R-loop sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 present genome-wide localization data with appropriate controls and statistical analysis. The enrichment at highly transcribed genes (C59) is supported by comparison to randomized controls (Figure 2D). The S-phase and CPT specificity (C60) and modest overlap with known R-loop sites (C61) are clearly documented.

results.result: R-loops accumulate at highly expressed genes in sae2Δ cells during CPT treatment. Using S9.6 antibody DRIP, sae2Δ cells showed ~2-fold higher R-loop levels at ADH1, ENO2, and FBA1 loci compared to wild-type. The signal was reduced by Sen1 overexpression and sensitive to RNaseH treatment in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 provide direct evidence of R-loop accumulation using the established S9.6 antibody method. The RNaseH sensitivity control (C64) confirms signal specificity, and the rescue by Sen1 overexpression (C63) is consistent with the genetic data. Quantitative measurements at multiple loci strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: RNA Pol II stalling is increased at highly expressed genes in sae2Δ strains during CPT treatment. Without DNA damage, all strains showed similar RNA Pol II occupancy. With CPT in S phase, wild-type showed 1.5-2-fold increased occupancy while sae2Δ exhibited 2.5-5.5-fold increases. Sen1 overexpression in sae2Δ reduced polymerase occupancy to wild-type levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 provide quantitative ChIP data showing differential RNA Pol II accumulation. The no-damage control (C65) establishes baseline equivalence, and the CPT-induced differences (C66-C67) are substantial. The rescue by Sen1 overexpression (C68) links polymerase stalling to the genetic rescue phenotype. Multiple loci were examined with appropriate replication.

results.result: CPT induces RNA Pol II stalling at Sen1-dependent genes in sae2Δ cells. Stalling was observed at PDC1 and NRD1 genes (known Sen1 targets) and at snoRNA genes SNR13, SNR5, and TRS31, which exhibit Sen1-dependent termination and R-loop phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 extend the RNA Pol II stalling observations to additional genomic loci with established Sen1 dependence. The consistency with prior literature on these specific genes strengthens the mechanistic interpretation. However, the stalling levels were noted to be lower than at the primary loci examined.

results.result: Sen1 recruitment to transcription sites is independent of Sae2. ChIP experiments showed Sen1 present at ADH1, ENO2, and FBA1 sites in sae2Δ cells, indicating Sae2-independent binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 address the epistatic relationship between Sen1 and Sae2. The demonstration that Sen1 is present at damage sites in the absence of Sae2 (C71) supports the interpretation that Sen1 acts in a parallel or downstream pathway. The ChIP data directly tests this relationship.

results.result: Senataxin overexpression rescues CPT sensitivity in CtIP-depleted human cells. CtIP depletion greatly reduced CPT survival, which was rescued by wild-type CtIP re-expression or Senataxin overexpression, but not by PCF11. DRB pre-treatment also partially rescued CPT sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 demonstrate conservation of the genetic interaction in human cells. The complete rescue by Senataxin (C75) parallels the yeast Sen1 results. The lack of PCF11 effect (C76) shows species-specific differences. The DRB rescue (C77) confirms transcription-dependence in human cells. Clonogenic survival assays provide quantitative data.

results.result: R-loop accumulation at laser-induced damage sites is increased in CtIP-depleted cells and rescued by Senataxin. Using RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry as an R-loop sensor, CtIP-depleted cells showed higher recruitment intensity compared to wild-type, which was reduced to wild-type levels by Senataxin expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 use live-cell imaging with an established R-loop sensor to demonstrate increased R-loops in CtIP-depleted cells. The rescue by Senataxin (C80) directly links the genetic suppression to R-loop resolution. The inference about R-loop levels (C79) is reasonable given the sensor's mechanism, though indirect.

results.result: CtIP nuclease activity is required for preventing R-loop accumulation at damage sites. The nuclease-deficient NA/HA mutant of CtIP failed to reduce RNaseH recruitment to damage sites in CtIP-depleted cells, indicating nuclease activity is necessary for R-loop processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 provide critical mechanistic insight using a separation-of-function mutant. The failure of the nuclease-dead mutant to complement (C81) directly implicates CtIP's catalytic activity. The inference about nuclease function (C82) is well-supported by this genetic evidence.

results.result: Transcription inhibition and Senataxin depletion affect R-loop accumulation. DRB pre-treatment rescued R-loop accumulation in CtIP-depleted cells, and Senataxin-depleted cells showed increased R-loop formation after laser damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 provide complementary evidence for transcription-dependence and Senataxin function. The DRB rescue (C83) confirms active transcription is required for the R-loop phenotype. The Senataxin depletion result (C84) is consistent with its known role in R-loop resolution and validates the experimental system.

results.result: XPG depletion increases R-loops, but concurrent CtIP/XPG depletion shows wild-type R-loop levels. XPG-depleted cells accumulated more R-loops after laser damage, but double depletion of CtIP and XPG resulted in R-loop levels comparable to wild-type untreated cells. This suggests R-loops either don't form efficiently or aren't recognized efficiently in the double mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 present a paradoxical observation that is difficult to interpret. While the data appear robust, the explanation (C87) is speculative. The authors propose two alternative hypotheses but cannot distinguish between them with the current data. This unexpected result requires additional experiments to resolve the mechanism, such as examining RNA polymerase occupancy or using alternative R-loop detection methods in the double mutant.

results.result: CtIP-depleted cells show elevated R-loops throughout the cell cycle, requiring CtIP nuclease activity. FACS analysis with RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry showed statistically significant increases in all cell cycle phases in CtIP-depleted cells. The nuclease-deficient NA/HA mutant showed identical R-loop levels to CtIP-depleted cells, indicating nuclease activity is necessary even without exogenous damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 extend R-loop observations to undamaged cells using a different methodology (FACS vs. microscopy). The cell cycle analysis (C88) shows the phenotype is not S-phase specific for endogenous R-loops. The nuclease mutant result (C89) reinforces the mechanistic conclusion from C81-C82. The inference about nuclease requirement (C90) is well-supported.

results.result: S9.6 immunofluorescence confirms elevated R-loops in CtIP- or XPG-depleted cells, with lower levels in double-depleted cells. Undamaged CtIP- or XPG-depleted cells showed significantly more R-loops than wild-type by S9.6 staining. Concurrent CtIP/XPG depletion resulted in lower R-loop accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 validate the FACS and laser damage results using an independent antibody-based method. The consistency across multiple detection methods strengthens confidence in the R-loop accumulation phenotype. The double depletion result (C92) reproduces the paradoxical observation from C86, confirming it is not method-specific.

results.result: CtIP depletion alters transcription patterns, with changes enriched at R-loop-prone genomic regions. RNA-seq showed CtIP depletion altered ~16% of transcripts (5,013 total). CPT treatment affected 2,443 transcripts, with >60% overlapping R-loop-prone regions (versus <40% for random genes). CtIP depletion effects also showed ~50% overlap with R-loop-prone regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 provide genome-wide transcriptional profiling with appropriate statistical analysis. The enrichment of affected genes at R-loop-prone regions (C95-C96) is statistically significant compared to randomized controls. This correlation supports a functional link between CtIP, R-loops, and transcription, though causality cannot be definitively established from correlation alone.

results.result: R-loops increase at an inducible locus (Sγ3) with transcription, with greater accumulation in CtIP-depleted cells. DRIP-qPCR at the doxycycline-inducible Sγ3 locus showed R-loop increases with transcription in wild-type cells, with much larger increases in CtIP-depleted cells despite similar transcript levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 use an inducible system to directly test the relationship between transcription and R-loop formation. The control showing similar transcript levels (C98) is important for ruling out indirect effects through altered transcription. The larger increase in CtIP-depleted cells supports a direct role in R-loop processing.

results.result: Endogenous R-loops accumulate at the β-actin gene in CtIP- or XPG-depleted cells. DRIP-qPCR showed higher RNA-DNA hybrids at β-actin in CtIP-depleted cells without exogenous damage, reducible to wild-type levels by RNaseH overexpression. XPG depletion showed even higher R-loop levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 examine endogenous R-loops at a specific, well-characterized locus. The RNaseH rescue (C100) confirms signal specificity. The comparison with XPG (C101) suggests both nucleases contribute to R-loop processing, with XPG potentially having a larger role at this locus.

results.result: R-loops accumulate at the RPL13A gene in CtIP- or XPG-depleted cells, requiring CtIP nuclease activity. DRIP-qPCR at three RPL13A locations showed significantly higher R-loops in CtIP-depleted cells, reduced by RNaseH overexpression or in vitro treatment. XPG depletion also showed high R-loops. The nuclease-deficient NA/HA CtIP mutant showed 1.5-2-fold higher R-loops than wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 provide detailed analysis at another endogenous locus with multiple primer sets and controls. The RNaseH controls (C103, in vitro treatment in supplement) confirm specificity. The nuclease mutant result (C105) is consistent with earlier findings and reinforces the mechanistic model. The examination of multiple sites within the gene strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Senataxin occupancy increases at R-loop sites in CtIP- or XPG-depleted cells. ChIP-qPCR showed 3-5-fold increased Senataxin occupancy at the inducible Sγ3 locus with depletion of either CtIP or XPG.
results.evaluation: Claim C106 demonstrates that Senataxin is recruited to sites with elevated R-loops, consistent with its role in R-loop resolution. The similar effect with CtIP or XPG depletion suggests both nucleases function in the same pathway. This result parallels the yeast Sen1 ChIP data (C71) and supports the model that helicases are recruited to process R-loops.

results.result: CtIP and XPG depletion reduce DNA break formation after CPT treatment. Alkaline comet assays showed CPT generated marked DNA break increases in wild-type cells, with ~75% reduction by DRB pre-treatment. CtIP depletion significantly reduced break accumulation after CPT. XPG depletion showed fewer breaks, and double CtIP/XPG depletion showed no increase in breaks with CPT. The nuclease-deficient NA/HA CtIP mutant showed large reduction in breaks.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 provide critical evidence that CtIP and XPG promote DNA break formation, likely through their nuclease activities. The comet assay data are quantitative and include appropriate controls (DRB for transcription-dependence, nuclease mutant for mechanism). The paradoxical observation that nuclease-deficient cells have fewer breaks despite more R-loops supports the model that nuclease cleavage converts R-loops into breaks.

results.result: Single-strand breaks at the RPL13A gene are reduced in CtIP-depleted cells. Ligation-mediated PCR showed spontaneous single-strand breaks on the RPL13A template strand, with 40-50% reduction upon CtIP depletion.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 provides locus-specific validation of the comet assay results using a different methodology. The LM-PCR approach allows strand-specific detection of breaks at a defined genomic location. The 40-50% reduction is consistent with the comet assay data and supports the model that CtIP generates breaks at R-loop sites.

results.result: Sae2/CtIP functions at transcription-associated lesions in addition to its role in double-strand break resection. The collective experimental evidence suggests Sae2/CtIP is not only a DSB resection factor but also functions at transcription-associated lesions in eukaryotic cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 represents the primary conclusion of the manuscript, synthesizing results from multiple experimental systems (yeast and human cells) and approaches (genetics, ChIP, R-loop detection, break analysis). The evidence from C37-C112 collectively supports this conclusion through: (1) genetic interactions with R-loop processing factors, (2) localization to transcribed genes, (3) R-loop accumulation in mutants, (4) transcription-dependence of phenotypes, and (5) requirement for nuclease activity.

results.result: The authors propose a model where 5' flap endonucleases (CtIP/XPG) process nascent R-loops by cleaving 5' flap structures, stabilizing the RNA-DNA hybrid and facilitating helicase-mediated removal. The model suggests nascent R-loops are topologically constrained and small, becoming accessible to helicases after nuclease cleavage releases tension in the DNA strand.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C121-C124, and C126 present a mechanistic model that is speculative and not directly tested. While the model is consistent with the observation that nuclease-deficient cells have more R-loops but fewer breaks (supporting the idea that cleavage stabilizes R-loops), key predictions are not experimentally validated. The model relies heavily on the paradoxical double mutant phenotype (C86-C87), which itself lacks a definitive explanation. Direct biochemical evidence for 5' flap cleavage at R-loops or demonstration that cleavage facilitates helicase access would be needed to support this model.
